stem: A task has distinct phases with different requirements — extract, then validate, then format, then synthesize. When is prompt chaining preferable to one big prompt?

options.label: A
options.body: Chain when the task has distinct phases: each step gets a smaller focused prompt, intermediate results can be validated, and steps can be retried independently.
options.rationale: Correct. Prompt chaining suits multi-phase tasks — higher accuracy per step, validation between steps, independent retries, and even different models per step. Use a single prompt only when the task is cohesive.

options.label: B
options.body: Never chain the phases — a single comprehensive prompt that covers extract, validate, format, and synthesize all at once is always the more reliable choice to make.
options.rationale: One big prompt handling distinct phases dilutes focus and can't validate intermediate results.

options.label: C
options.body: Chain the steps only when the goal is to reduce token cost, and never do it for the sake of improving per-step accuracy or enabling validation between the phases.
options.rationale: Chaining's main benefits are focus and validation per step; cost optimization (different models per step) is secondary.

options.label: D
options.body: Chain the phases only in the specific case where a single combined prompt would exceed the model's context window, and otherwise keep it all in one prompt.
options.rationale: Distinct phases justify chaining regardless of whether one prompt would fit.

stem: A coordinator is handed an open-ended task whose sub-structure isn't clear upfront. Should it commit to a fixed decomposition or decompose dynamically, and why?

options.label: A
options.body: Decompose dynamically — for open-ended tasks the right split only emerges as work proceeds; fixed decomposition suits predictable tasks.
options.rationale: Correct. Fixed decomposition fits predictable tasks; dynamic decomposition fits open-ended exploration where you can't predict the structure at design time.

options.label: B
options.body: Always commit to a fixed decomposition up front for the sake of consistency, regardless of how open-ended or unpredictable the task's structure turns out to be.
options.rationale: A fixed split on an unknown structure locks the agent into the wrong subtasks.

options.label: C
options.body: Avoid decomposing the task at all and instead handle the entire open-ended request within a single large prompt from start to finish.
options.rationale: Open-ended tasks benefit from decomposition; one prompt dilutes attention and misses branches.

options.label: D
options.body: Spawn exactly one subagent for each sentence in the request as the mechanism for dividing up the open-ended work among workers.
options.rationale: Arbitrary fan-out isn't decomposition by requirement; it multiplies cost without matching the task's real structure.
